title: Mars: A Light That Answers
ending: We’re through the orbiter’s hatch together, with our specimens and the picture from our table. The light that answered us has become our way home.

steps.message: Radio. Replace the damaged detachable lead; the radio itself is repaired, not duplicated.
Solar charger. Connect the salvaged collector to its compatible storage unit.
Solar radio. Fit an internal power supply to the radio.
Placed. We hear you. That light above the ridge means someone is still there—and now we can answer.
We take the useful equipment onward to somewhere to come back to, leaving the earlier work where it stands.
Meltwater. A recovered enclosed melt head collects water; exposed liquid on Mars would not behave like an Earth puddle.
Filtered water. The mission filter processes this known source inside its enclosed vessel; not real water-safety advice.
Water canister. Seal the water against dust and evaporation.
Seed tray. The tray contains prepared terrestrial growing medium.
Watered seed tray. Water the prepared tray.
Sprouted tray. Time passes in the warm pressurized cabin; no instant real germination is implied.
Propagator. Protect the living tray from the disturbed entrance air.
Pressure patch. Prepare a compatible patch for the damaged outer vestibule.
Sealed panel. Work the compatible seam closed.
Vestibule. Fit the repaired outer entrance around the existing hatch.
Anchored vestibule. Anchor the fabric structure to its prepared footings.

Insulated vestibule. Wrap the outer structure; the inner cabin still supplies pressure and life support. The entry is weather-tight, the water is stored, and the little tray has a sheltered home. We have somewhere to come back to.
We take the useful equipment onward to the route out, leaving the earlier work where it stands. We collect the things needed for this scene along the way.
Rover. A wheeled chassis is a recognizable rover with unfilled component slots.
Drive unit. Connect the matching controller to the motor.
Drive unit fitted to Rover.
Solar charger fitted to Rover.
Seat harness fitted to Rover.
Bearing scope. Read a direction while sighting a landmark.
Field camera. A stable camera can make repeatable wide views.
Panorama. Record the visible route, not a claim that it is safe to cross.
Survey map. Mark the observed landmarks on the map.
Bearing map. Add the observed bearings to the existing map. The rover can carry us, and the bearings give us a route to follow. Now let’s find our missing crew.
We take the useful equipment onward to what the cliff can tell us, leaving the earlier work where it stands. We collect the things needed for this scene along the way.
Ice sample. Collect ice from the exposed outcrop beside the current viewpoint.
Sealed ice sample. Seal the actual specimen in its jar.
Catalogued ice sample. Retain provenance on the specimen container.
Ice photograph. Photograph through the transparent jar.
Telescope. Align the recovered optical components.
Field telescope. Give the optical tube a stable support.
Telescope camera. Attach the camera to the supported optics.
Cliff photograph. Record the layered cliff at the route's far side.
Annotated map. Add this new observation to the same route map.
Ice core. Recover a short core with its layer order retained.
Core rack. Support the fragile sample for a profile photograph.
Scaled core. Place a visible scale beside the core without treating the label as a discovery.

Core profile. Record visible structure; the image is evidence, not a proof of ancient life. The ice has its label and photograph; the cliff has given our map more detail. We can carry the evidence without pretending we know the whole story.
The mapped instrument apron is a short drive from the outcrop. We take the field kit and leave the sampling bench where it stands. We collect the things needed for this scene along the way.
Weather station. Restore the missing wind vane to the complete calibrated sensor mast. The existing sensors need their logger and power connection, not rebuilding.
Sensor logger fitted to Weather station.
Solar charger fitted to Weather station.
Weather record. On the open apron, the restored station records a period of changing weather. The passage of observation time is narrated.
Weather route map. Compare the new weather record with the terrain already mapped to choose a visible route toward the relay.
Dust screen. Fit filter mesh into the vented equipment enclosure, making a dust screen for the exposed controller.

Protected controller. Enclose the controller behind the fitted dust screen while retaining its designed cooling vents. The station has given us a weather-informed route, and the spare controller is protected. We can move on without forgetting how quickly this place changes.
The weather record gives us a route to the relay knoll. We bring the map and leave the station measuring conditions behind us. We collect the things needed for this scene along the way.
Relay. Replace the identified blown fuse in the intact relay transceiver. Its internal radio circuits are already assembled.
Directional antenna fitted to Relay.
Relay powerpack fitted to Relay.
Distress recording. From the clear relay knoll, the working relay receives and stores the missing survey crew’s message.

Rescue route. Locate the crew’s reported landmark on the weather route map. The signal becomes a route to people, not just a stronger radio. We have their voices—and a route to them. Their cabin is intact; it’s the drive that failed. Let’s bring them to shelter.

The message and map lead to the disabled crawler and the service refuge farther along the recovery route. We bring the rover and recovery kit; the working relay stays on its knoll. We collect the things needed for this scene along the way.
Serviced drive. Inspect and service the supplied replacement drive.
Replacement drive. Fit its matched coupling.
Crawler. Replace the failed drive module in the original crawler.
Prepared bed. Make a comfortable place for the exhausted crew.
Sealed refuge. Repair the shelter's documented torn outer seam.
Warm refuge. Connect its compatible heating socket; intact life support remains a recovered system.
Prepared refuge. Put the prepared bed inside the heated refuge.
Occupied refuge. Drive the repaired crawler along the short recovery route and bring its crew into the prepared refuge.
Warm soup. Warm the crew’s prepared food pouch with the compatible enclosed heater.
Hot meal flask. Keep the prepared food warm for the return journey.

Provisioned refuge. Give the sheltered crew the hot meal and let them settle after the difficult wait. Everyone is sheltered and fed. Our stocked mission habitat supports the months until the scheduled return window; we can prepare for it together, not race through chores in danger.
We collect the known equipment needed for this work and move to recovery camp. Earlier work stays where we left it. We collect the things needed for this scene along the way.
Workbench. Fit the stored legs to their worktop, making a shared workbench.
Bench lamp. Fit the movable lamp bracket to the existing portable lamp.
Lit workbench. Mount the lamp at the workbench so the crew can work together after dark.
Crew message. Record the sheltered crew’s message for their families.
Long range radio. Fit the directional antenna to the existing radio.
Antenna stand fitted to Long range radio.
Message home. Send the crew’s recorded message during the narrated contact interval. We have a lit bench to share, and our families have heard our voices. This is starting to feel like a camp again.

We gather beside the camp path for a short furniture pickup. The Cargo shoulder is within sight; the crew knows the way, and the camp remains our home for this first safe evening. We collect the things needed for this scene along the way.
Padded sling. Fit the pads around the recovery rope. The padded sling is ready to bring the furniture sled back from the Cargo shoulder.

Recovered mess crate. Fit the sling to the sled’s handling points. Together, the crew hand-hauls it along the short, firm camp path and unloads its folding mess crate beside camp. The table is back; the toolkit can release its transport fasteners.
Mess table. Release the transport fasteners with the toolkit and unfold the recovered crate into the crew’s mess table.
Personal table. Put the crew’s own photographs under the table’s clear protective cover.
Shared supper. The familiar insulated flask stands on the recovered table; the crew draw up together to share the soup it still holds.

Crew portrait. Take a photograph of the reunited crew around their recovered table, a personal image to carry home. Our own table, our pictures, all of us together on this first safe evening. Keep that portrait—we’ll want to remember more than the breakdown.
We collect the known equipment needed for this work and move to camp thermal workshop. Earlier work stays where we left it.
Placed.
Cooling trace. Run the wall sample through the chamber’s stored cooling cycle and keep the recorded trace.
Insulated wall sample. Wrap the test wall coupon with the mission insulation swatch for a comparison under the same chamber cycle.
Placed.
Insulated cooling trace. Repeat the same stored cooling cycle with the insulated wall sample.
Insulation comparison. Compare the bare and insulated sample traces from the same controlled cycle.
Screen pattern. Use the tested insulation material with the existing measured wall template to plan the removable screen.
Fitted blanket. Fit the blanket to the measured screen pattern.
Thermal screen. Secure the fitted insulating blanket in the removable screen frame.

Screened cabin. Fit the thermal screen over the cabin’s exposed service wall. The two chamber traces gave us a reason to fit this screen. The exposed service wall is covered; tonight the sleeping cabin feels more like ours.
We take the useful equipment onward to enough water to stay, leaving the earlier work where it stands. We collect the things needed for this scene along the way.
Circulating water loop. Attach the matched return hose to the complete circulation pump.
Heated melter. Connect the compatible heater to the sealed vessel.
Collected water. The local ice feed and enclosed apparatus produce a collected batch.
Process water. Run collected meltwater through the qualified process-water skid. This is water for the enclosed growing loop, not an unsupported drinking-water safety claim.
Water reserve. Fill the monitored process-water tank from the treatment skid.

Camp water system. Feed the closed camp water circuit from its protected reserve. The camp’s process-water loop is working again. We can supply the enclosed growing system without treating an unknown water sample as a promise of drinking safety.
We take the useful equipment onward to a meal that grew here, leaving the earlier work where it stands. We collect the things needed for this scene along the way.
Greenhouse. Repair the documented damaged panel seam in the otherwise intact greenhouse.
Planting bed. Fill the complete growing tray with the brought mission substrate.
Planted potatoes. Plant the stored seed potatoes in their prepared bed.
Irrigation line. Connect the growing circuit to the enclosed water system.
Watered potatoes. Supply the bed without flooding its roots.
Watered potatoes fitted to Greenhouse.
Powered grow light. Connect the lighting unit to its compatible power supply.
Powered grow light fitted to Greenhouse.
Circulation fan fitted to Greenhouse.
Potato harvest. After a narrated growing interval, gather the crop from the restored greenhouse.

Warm potatoes. Cook the harvest in the supplied food-safe heater attachment. After the growing weeks, a warm meal from our own greenhouse. The mission stores kept us fed; this tastes like something we made together.
We gather the known equipment for this nearby work. The larger expedition remains at its current camp or depot. We collect the things needed for this scene along the way.
Identified seedlings. Label the living seedlings kept alive since the landing; these are not new seed potatoes.
Supported seedlings. Fit the ready support lattice to the original tray so the seedlings can stand without crowding.
Framed diffuser. Fit the greenhouse’s compatible light diffuser into its stored frame.
Shelf shadow view. Photograph the empty nursery shelf under the existing light: the frame casts a sharp band of shadow.
Shadow layout. Mark where the frame shadows fall on the shelf grid; this diagnoses an obstruction, not a crop yield or safety threshold.
Positioned diffuser. Use the shadow layout to set the diffuser frame at the intended mounting position.
Positioned diffuser fitted to Greenhouse.

Camp nursery. Move the protected tray into the greenhouse nursery bay after a narrated visual check of the fitted diffuser against the shadow layout, not a quantitative light-sufficiency test. Future growth is narrated, not instantaneous. The little tray from landing has a supported place in the greenhouse nursery. We’re leaving something living for the next crew, not just repaired equipment.
Back at the camp machine shop, we bring the recovered crawler to the stored tools and stock. Here we can fit it for the field journey ahead. We collect the things needed for this scene along the way.
Padded carrier. Protect specimens from vibration.
Sample carrier. Close the carrier without sealing an unknown atmosphere inside a food container.
Mounting bracket. Make the specified carrier bracket from stock.
Mounted sample carrier. Fit the bracket for a rover-mounted specimen carrier.
Mounted sample carrier fitted to Crawler.
Machined axle. Machine the specified replacement axle using the stored design; not freeform precision from hand tools.
Wheel module. Make a ready-to-fit wheel and axle module.
Wheel module fitted to Crawler. The replacement wheel is fitted, and our samples have a protected carrier. The crawler can take the next leg with the things we worked to save.

The crawler takes us from the camp machine shop to the lava survey margin, on the wheel we fitted and with its sample carrier aboard. We stop at the overlook to survey the rough ground ahead. We collect the things needed for this scene along the way.
Scout. Fit purpose-built Mars rotor assemblies, not an Earth toy drone.
Scout battery fitted to Scout.
Scout panorama. Fly a short reconnaissance using the stored flight envelope; thin atmosphere limits performance.
Terrain model. Turn overlapping calibrated images into a local terrain model using recovered software.
Traverse map. Add the new local terrain observations to the route.
Marked traverse. Mark the identified route hazards, rather than inventing certainty beyond the surveyed area.
Marked traverse fitted to Crawler. The scout’s images have become a marked route for the crawler. A view from above helps—but we still need to look at the ground beneath our wheels.

We bring the wheel-equipped crawler along the surveyed leg to the shallow channel. From here, the marked approach still needs a closer look on the ground. We collect the things needed for this scene along the way.
Ground profile. Use the field probe to compare the near-surface layers at the approach; detailed testing and interpretation are abstracted.
Firm-ground route. Match the ground observations to the scout terrain model to identify a supported approach.
Crossing map. Mark the chosen approach on the route overlay.
Marked crossing. Place the marker according to the mapped approach, yielding a marked route for the crawler.

Placed. The approach is marked, and the crawler is here on the wheel we fitted at camp, with its sample carrier aboard. The checks cover this approach, not the whole channel. We can take the next leg together.

We follow the marked approach and continue on foot to the layered basin. The crawler brought our field kit out from camp; it waits at the channel approach with its fitted wheel and sample carrier. We collect the things needed for this scene along the way.
Lined core drill. Fit the sample liner without claiming perfect sterility.
Sediment core. In this fictional field record, a coarser-grained band lies between two fine-grained layers. The core preserves their order, but contains no dates.
Supported core. Support the layered material for inspection.

Grain images. The images show larger individual grains in the middle band and finer grains above and below. The difference is visible; these pictures alone establish neither what transported the grains nor any biological origin.
Retained sediment. Save a portion with its source identity.
Calibrated spectrometer. Use the supplied target to check the instrument's reference response.

Mineral spectrum. The single retained portion gives a scan with broad, overlapping features. This fictional field reading does not support a unique mineral identification; it stays in the record as an inconclusive result.
Sediment comparison. The images distinguish fine and coarse layers. The spectrum does not settle their origin. The comparison keeps the useful result and the inconclusive one side by side.

Layer interpretation. The earlier profile records layers in an ice exposure; this core records sediment at another site. Here, grain sizes differ from one layer to the next. Comparing the records does not establish a shared age or cause.

Basin field record. This fictional mission record preserves a coarse band between two fine-grained layers at the core site. Grain sizes and layer order are recorded; age and transport agent remain unresolved. Nearby exposures may help test a water-transport explanation. A coarse band lies between two finer ones. We can show that change, and we have kept the specimen; we cannot yet say what carried the grains here. Nearby, a rippled surface and a gravel ledge offer another comparison. Let’s take our question to them.
We gather the known equipment for this nearby work. The larger expedition remains at its current camp or depot. We collect the things needed for this scene along the way.
Ripple view. Record the rippled surface and its surroundings, not just an attractive crop of the pattern.
Gravel view. Record the rounded gravel in its rock matrix and the neighbouring layers.
Scaled gravel view. Add the in-scene scale reference to the image record so the pebble dimensions can be interpreted; capture and annotation are compressed.
Paired terrain views. Put the two source views beside each other: similar-looking surface patterns need not share one origin.
Deposition context. Place both sites on the terrain model; grain context and layer geometry matter more than a ripple silhouette.
Qualified basin story. Revise the earlier account: the gravel supports ancient transport by water; the rippled surface alone does not. We have an evidence-weighted history, not a life detection.
Comparison board. Mount the paired interpretation on the board with separate source positions and explicit uncertainty.
Sleeved comparison. Protect the annotated comparison for the journey home. The separate specimen case retains its source labels.
Ripple impression. Take a small dry impression preserving the ripple surface’s shape without pretending it is a water signature.
Ripple impression fitted to Two-cell comparison case.
Logged gravel chip. Attach the existing log’s precise ledge provenance to the already loose chip.

Logged gravel chip fitted to Two-cell comparison case. Those ripples alone don’t prove a river. The gravel and its setting tell a stronger ancient-water story; we’ve kept both sources distinct so others can examine our reasoning.

Leaving the basin work behind, we reach the old depot service approach. The permanent survey markers should distinguish its route from the wandering dark tracks. We collect the things needed for this scene along the way.
Standing route sign. Fit the intact directional sign to its matching stable foot.
Revealed socket mark. Clear loose dust from the accessible survey plate, exposing its surveyed route identifier. No digging near buried utilities.
Current marker view. Photograph the crossing tracks and faint survey sockets at the approach.
Registered route views. Register the current image against the original depot survey using permanent rocks and sockets, not transient tracks.

Track disagreement. The wandering fresh tracks and the earlier weather record show why surface marks cannot substitute for the engineered route. Treat them as surface change, not a shortcut to the depot.
Identified service route. Use the actual survey identifier to locate the original service approach. Wind evidence explained the misleading marks; it did not prove a route safe.
Depot route sign. Set the sign to indicate the surveyed service approach so later cargo trips do not repeat this puzzle.
Protected controller fitted to Depot hauler.
Hauler platform fitted to Depot hauler.

Depot cargo shuttle. Bring the restored cargo hauler along the identified existing service approach during narrated travel. The permanent markers led us back to the service route, not the wandering dark tracks. That controller we protected now runs the hauler that will carry our samples to the ship.

We follow the permanent markers to the old ascent depot. Beside the waiting vehicle stands the oxygen plant we came to restore. The hauler we brought along the service approach, running on our protected controller, is ready for the specimens’ last stretch.
Oxygen plant. Restore the recovered solid-oxide oxygen-generation module and its matched controller.
Filtered intake fitted to Oxygen plant.
Placed.

Serviced oxygen module. Use the qualified depot loading equipment to service the ascent module from the working plant. Process settings and handling operations remain outside the game. The restored depot plant has serviced the ascent oxygen module through its designed equipment. That work now has a real place in the vehicle waiting for us.
We take the useful equipment onward to a ship with an unfinished job, leaving the earlier work where it stands. We collect the things needed for this scene along the way.
Ascent cabin. Replace the documented failed hatch seal.
Docking ring fitted to Ascent cabin.
Serviced oxygen module fitted to Ascent cabin.
Flight console fitted to Ascent cabin.
Flight seat fitted to Ascent cabin.

Cabin test record. Run the vehicle's built-in depot test under remote supervision. The cabin is restored, and its built-in test record is in hand. Now we can turn from repairing our ship to agreeing where it will meet the orbiter.
We take the useful equipment onward to a moving meeting place, leaving the earlier work where it stands. We collect the things needed for this scene along the way.
Ranging link. Restore the depot's compatible ranging interface.
Aligned star tracker. Check its reference alignment using the supplied target.
Sky fix. Observe the visible star field; do not navigate by an invented Earth constellation shortcut.
Ground reference. Establish the site's observed reference orientation.
Timing station. Record beacon timing against the recovered clock.
Beacon times. Record the actual received beacon sequence.
Orbiter pass prediction. Compare observations against the transmitted orbital data.
Rendezvous solution. The certified navigation software combines measured reference and orbital data.

Agreed rendezvous. Exchange and verify the calculated meeting plan with the orbiter. Our clocks, observations and beacon measurements have become an agreed meeting. After all that waiting, we know which light we’re going toward.
We take the useful equipment onward to what we take with us, leaving the earlier work where it stands. We collect the things needed for this scene along the way.
Secured cart. Fit the cargo strap to the recovered depot hauler that we brought along the surveyed approach.
Return capsule. Fit the specimen capsule's vibration protection.
Catalogued ice sample fitted to Return capsule.
Retained sediment fitted to Return capsule.
Archival recorder. Fit the compatible archive medium to its reader.
Family record. Save the recovered crew’s table portrait alongside the earlier personal recording for the journey home.
Geology archive. Store the recorded observations and explicit uncertainties.
Complete field archive. Keep the earlier profile with the later interpretation.
Complete field archive fitted to Return capsule.
Two-cell comparison case fitted to Return capsule.
Sleeved comparison fitted to Return capsule.
Specimen cart. Secure the return capsule for transfer.

Camp handover beacon. Leave the next crew the maintenance card, including the living nursery and the restored greenhouse fittings, at the camp beacon. The specimens, their records and our portrait are ready to travel. The handover beacon tells the next crew what we leave behind—including a living nursery.
We take the useful equipment onward to a light that answers, leaving the earlier work where it stands. We collect the things needed for this scene along the way.
Ascent vehicle. Mate the already qualified vehicle modules at their designed interface.
Capsule dock. Prepare the designed return-capsule mount.
Loaded capsule dock. Transfer the secured capsule to its ship mount.
Loaded ascent vehicle. Install the specimen cargo without replacing the vehicle.
Rendezvous program. Load the accepted navigation and telemetry plan into its designed recorder.
Flight ready vehicle. Load the agreed flight plan into the existing ship.
Ascending vehicle. A narrated supervised ascent compresses the flight; no real launch procedure is provided.
Docked vehicle. The agreed rendezvous meets the waiting orbital cabin.

Returned capsule. Cross the hatch together; the saved specimens and records remain tangible cargo. We’re through the orbiter’s hatch together, with our specimens and the picture from our table. The light that answered us has become our way home.
We’re through the orbiter’s hatch together, with our specimens and the picture from our table. The light that answered us has become our way home.
